title: Nepal Police command meets for hours amid fears of IG sacking - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal Police command meets for hours amid fears of IG sacking  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal Police chief Dan Bahadur Karki convened an emergency and unusually lengthy meeting of senior officers on Thursday, amid rumours that the government was preparing to remove him from office.

The policy coordination committee meeting at the police headquarters in Naxal, Kathmandu, ran from 2pm to 7pm. It brought together senior superintendents of police, deputy inspectors general and officials of higher ranks serving in the Capital. Officials said the meeting lasted longer than previous policy coordination sessions as participants raised questions and offered their views.

Deputy Inspector General Abi Narayan Kafle, the central police spokesperson, said officers discussed the current law and order situation, contemporary issues and subjects circulating on social media.

“Everyone’s views on the issue were heard,” he told Kantipur. Kafle said that participants discussed what they considered deliberate attempts to spread misleading information and undermine the force’s reputation, professionalism and performance.

A statement issued after the meeting said the organisation would investigate and take legal action against those attempting to drag the law enforcement agency into controversy. “Some individuals believe they can act against the government by drawing the security agency into controversy,” it said, adding that action would proceed under prevailing laws.

The meeting came amid reports that the government wanted Karki to step down. Some officials at the Prime Minister’s Office are reportedly dissatisfied with his handling of investigations involving high-profile figures, particularly his insistence on following the legal procedure of arrest.

Karki has also faced public allegations from Khagendra Sunar, a lawmaker from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party, over alleged irregularities in the purchase of uniform for temporary recruits deployed for the March 5 election. The Public Accounts Committee has formed a subcommittee led by RSP lawmaker Manish Jha to examine the procurement.

Meanwhile, reports have emerged about conversations between Karki and Inam Sapkota, a middleman under investigation for allegations related to money laundering and banking offences. Sapkota reportedly has cultivated relationships with judges, senior Nepal Police and Armed Police Force officials, lawyers and ruling party leaders, claiming his close links to the prime minister and the US embassy.

According to an officer who attended Thursday’s meeting, Karki said the force was facing attacks and urged colleagues to remain united. He also named some suspects outside the organisation and warned officers against taking internal matters outside, the officer said.

Participants discussed whether they should approach the Prime Minister’s Office to clarify issues raised publicly. Most agreed that officers should act together when the institution’s standing was at stake, the participant said. Others argued that individuals should answer allegations concerning them personally, while the police organisation should respond to matters affecting the force as a whole.

One senior officer asked Karki whether anyone in the government had asked him to resign. Karki, according to a participant, replied that the reports were untrue and that nobody had asked him to step down.

“The decision was that everyone would stand together to protect the organisation’s image and reputation and ensure that law and order is not affected,” the officer said.

On Wednesday, Karki addressed police chiefs from the Kathmandu valley, provincial police offices, training centres and district offices through a virtual meeting, taking his remarks down to inspector-level office chiefs.

Karki warned officers not to turn against colleagues, alleging that relations among officers of the same batch had also become less cordial. At Thursday’s meeting, he reiterated that associating with people of poor conduct would not benefit officers.

title: PM Shah floated the idea of Nepal-India-China cooperation on climate. Why is the government slow to reach out to the neighbours? - The Kathmandu Post
description: PM Shah floated the idea of Nepal-India-China cooperation on climate. Why is the government slow to reach out to the neighbours?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
A month after Prime Minister Balendra Shah proposed establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism (HCRM) involving Nepal, India and China, the initiative has made little diplomatic headway, with the two ministries concerned still working on a concept note and no formal proposal submitted yet to either neighbour.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment are consulting relevant agencies to develop the proposal, but the initiative has yet to move beyond the preparatory stage.

Shah floated the proposal in his address to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 24. The idea received a positive response from several quarters, albeit with cautious optimism given the volatile and unpredictable relationship between India and China. Nepal, meanwhile, has comparatively fewer bilateral issues with its immediate neighbours.

The proposal followed the devastating Bhotekoshi flood in the Nepal-Tibet region on August 26, which killed 1,550 people, with more than 5,500 others still unaccounted for. The disaster also caused property damage estimated by the government at $4.7 billion.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to nearly two billion people, Shah said while presenting the idea of the HCRM. The mountain range provides water, sustains ecosystems and agriculture, and supports livelihoods far beyond Nepal.

“The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system. That is why, as an urgent first step, we propose that we establish a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China. Through this mechanism, let us share satellite data and expertise. Let us monitor dangerous glacial lakes. Let us strengthen joint early-warning systems,” Shah said in his address, which received considerable attention and was widely praised as one of the most powerful speeches delivered by a Nepali prime minister in recent years.

He also called for cross-border coordination and assistance during disasters, proposing that the Himalayas become a laboratory for international cooperation rather than a frontier marked by fragmented information.

However, nearly a month after the proposal was formally presented at the General Assembly, there has been little progress in bilateral engagement with India and China.

A senior foreign ministry official said that the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment was preparing a concept note and consulting relevant agencies on how to establish the mechanism.

“We have received correspondence just this week from the foreign ministry. We will consult with various agencies and will get back to them,” a joint secretary at the environment ministry told the Post. The foreign ministry, referring to the prime minister’s statement in New York, had asked the ministry to prepare a concept note, the official added.

The environment ministry has been asked to develop a proposal for establishing the mechanism and seek technical inputs.

New Delhi has not officially commented on Nepal's proposal. However, two former Indian diplomats familiar with the thinking within India's establishment told the Post that Delhi was positive about establishing a mechanism focused on sharing information, particularly for early-warning systems.

Despite the initial optimism, Nepal has yet to formally approach either New Delhi or Beijing with a detailed proposal for establishing the mechanism.

“We do not know whether the idea was discussed with India and China before the prime minister's address at the UNGA. It could come up during Prime Minister Shah's upcoming visit to India,” said a former Indian ambassador to Kathmandu.

A Nepali diplomat questioned how any of the neighbours could be expected to respond formally without first receiving an official proposal from Kathmandu.

“The prime minister made the proposal during his statement at the United Nations General Assembly, which is a multilateral forum. On the basis of that statement, Nepal needs to formally write to both Delhi and Beijing, explaining the rationale, objectives and other details of the proposed mechanism,” the diplomat said. “Only then can we receive official feedback. Without submitting a formal proposal, how can we ask for their comments and reactions?”

China, meanwhile, has expressed a general willingness to cooperate on climate change and disaster management, without explicitly endorsing the proposed trilateral mechanism.

On September 2, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference in Beijing: “Climate change is a common challenge facing all humanity. No country can stay immune from such risks. China will continue to work with the international community to strengthen exchanges and cooperation and effectively prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change.”

Former chief secretary and foreign secretary Shanker Das Bairagi said he knows little about the proposed mechanism's operational framework, structure, objectives or other practical details.

“Now the onus is on us to determine what kind of mechanism we need to establish. Accordingly, we have to make a proposal to India and China. However, I do not think there has been much inter-agency coordination and cooperation in this regard,” Bairagi said. “This is an issue related to access to water, lives and livelihoods.”

Bairagi also warned that the mechanism could trigger a geopolitical debate because its scope includes Tibet. China considers Tibet a sensitive region and places restrictions on access for foreign scientists, researchers and experts conducting geological studies.

India, on the other hand, could be more receptive to the idea, Bairagi said, noting that New Delhi had already agreed to establish a BIMSTEC Himalayan Science Council.

In 2017, a meeting of the BIMSTEC expert group on the security implications of ecological and environmental degradation in the Himalayan region decided to establish the council to comprehensively study the health of the Himalayan ecosystem and promote scientific cooperation among institutions in member states.

The meeting also decided to establish a BIMSTEC expert group to prepare a concept paper and plan of action. Experts subsequently met in 2021 and 2023, but the council has yet to be institutionalised.

An official at the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, where the idea of establishing the HCRM is being considered, said India and China had demonstrated a degree of convergence on climate change issues at international forums despite their differences on other matters. This, the official said, could provide an opportunity for greater cooperation under Nepal's proposal.

Indian media outlets, including The Indian Express , have highlighted the proposal and its implications for India's regional climate diplomacy. India has experience sharing hydrological information with China and providing disaster relief to Nepal. However, sharing real-time river-flow data, satellite imagery and glacier-monitoring information could raise strategic and national-security concerns, particularly amid unresolved border tensions between India and China.

On September 2, the Chinese foreign ministry said Beijing had shared satellite imagery, hydrological information and early-warning information with Nepal following the August disaster. It also expressed its willingness to continue cooperating with Nepal on disaster prevention and mitigation.

The statement indicated China's support for bilateral disaster cooperation with Nepal, but it did not amount to a formal acceptance of the proposed three-country mechanism.

A senior foreign ministry official told the Post that the proposal might need to be developed by the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, rather than the foreign ministry taking the lead.

A climate change expert said the mechanism would need a clear framework for funding, data sharing, scientific monitoring and emergency coordination, particularly given the geopolitical sensitivities surrounding access to information on shared rivers and glaciers.

A senior foreign ministry official said the environment ministry was preparing a proposal in consultation with relevant stakeholders.

title: Opinion | Nepal’s government needs to vet public appointments before announcing them - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal’s government needs to vet public appointments before announcing them  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In May, the Balendra Shah government emptied 1,594 public positions overnight , through one sweeping ordinance. Classrooms, clinics and offices felt the gap, and the country held its breath to see who would sit down next. The question that emerged then was: What would guarantee that the new officials would not simply be political appointees close to the ruling party? It was a fair question then, and it is a fair one still.

Six months on, we know some of the answers, and they are troubling. A government that sweeps a house this loudly must lay the table with care. Too many of its choices were made before anyone asked the hard question: Was every candidate checked before the cabinet recommended them?

Take Lumbini. On October 16, the cabinet named Ani Choying Drolma vice-chair of the Lumbini Development Trust, filling a post that had been empty for nearly five months . She says every question about her has been answered, yet the Post found the record less certain . A money-laundering inquiry from 2018 and citizenship doubts from 2019 remain formally unresolved . Nobody has proved wrongdoing. But whoever leads the trust should arrive with every question closed. Instead, protests have run since October 17 , and police arrested a campaign chair . Nobody needed this scene.

The ambassadorial nominees list tells a similar tale. The foreign ministry invited applications and drew more than 4,400 , a welcome break after some seats had sat empty for nearly 10 months . Then the 13 names reached Parliament, where complaints were waiting . A hearing committee dominated by the ruling party turned down two nominees , a first for any House committee. Its chair said Giribahadur Sunar, proposed for Saudi Arabia, was removed after a woman complained of violence against her and told her story by video. Sunar has asked his accusers to produce evidence. Chudamani Kharel, proposed for Malaysia, did not meet the qualifications the rules demand. Jigyan Kumar Thapa, proposed for Japan, is on hold for his alleged citizenship of Japan. He says he gave up his permanent residency there in March . Party sources told the Post that Sunar and Kharel were seen as close to the prime minister's camp , and that Thapa’s name came on the Speaker’s behalf.

The committee did the checking the ministry should have done. The woman who told her story to strangers on a screen deserves a state that listens before it announces a name. A foreign ministry official called the process trial and error . Nepal’s face abroad cannot be chosen by trial.

The ruling Rastriya Swantantra Party calls the rejections proof that Parliament can check the executive, and that is fair. The lesson holds either way: a check at the last gate cannot stand in for a check at the first.

This problem can be mended in weeks. First, suspend the Lumbini appointment and give the money-laundering department and the citizenship authorities a specific timeframe, say 30 days, to publish their findings. If Drolma is cleared, she returns with her name restored. If she is not, Lumbini is spared a deep wound. Second, the foreign ministry should send the hearing committee every paper it asks for on Thapa, and fill the Saudi and Malaysian posts from applicants already screened, after background checks.

Third, make vetting a habit. Before any cabinet recommendation for a public post, state investigative bodies should check citizenship, taxes, financial records, conduct complaints and conflicts of interest, and pass the findings to the hearing committee. Publish the shortlist and the reasons for every pick, in every body the ordinance emptied.

title: In Nepal, police chief holds meeting amid resignation rumors — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, police chief holds meeting amid resignation rumors — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS

Nepal Police chief Dan Bahadur Karki held an emergency five-hour meeting with senior officers in Kathmandu amid reports that the government may be seeking his resignation. The meeting at police headquarters in the Naxal area lasted from 2:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m., Kathmandu Post reports.

Discussion of the police's reputation

Senior superintendents of police, deputy inspectors general and other high-ranking officials working in the capital took part in the meeting. Central police spokesperson, Deputy Inspector General Abhi Narayan Kafle, said participants discussed the law-and-order situation, current issues and topics circulating on social media.

According to him, the officers also spoke about what they believe is the targeted dissemination of misleading information damaging the reputation, professionalism and work of the police. In a statement following the meeting, law enforcement officials said they would investigate attempts to draw the agency into controversies and take legal action in accordance with current legislation.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Rumors of a possible resignation

The meeting took place amid reports that the government allegedly wants Karki to leave his post. According to the publication, some officials in the prime minister's office are dissatisfied with his approach to investigations involving influential individuals, particularly his insistence on following procedure during arrests.

One meeting participant said that Karki spoke of attacks on the police and called on colleagues to maintain unity. When a senior officer asked whether anyone in the government had asked him to resign, the police chief, according to the participant, answered in the negative.

Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Khagendra Sunar publicly made allegations against Karki regarding possible violations in the procurement of uniforms for temporary recruits involved in the March 5 elections. The Public Accounts Committee established a subcommittee to examine the procurement. Separately, media reports emerged about Karki's conversations with Inam Sapkota, a middleman under investigation on suspicion of money laundering and banking offenses.

title: Nepal Bar Association calls for investigation into reports about judges — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal Bar Association calls for investigation into reports about judges — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the Bar Association called for an investigation into Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma and Justice Hari Prasad Phuyal after information emerged about their connection with Inam Sapkota. He was detained on September 27, and The Kathmandu Post describes Sapkota as a possible intermediary.

According to the publication, investigators are examining Sapkota's contacts with serving and former judges, senior police officials, lawmakers and government representatives. Earlier, information emerged about his ties to former Chief Justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana and dismissed Armed Police Force Deputy Inspector General Banshiraj Dahal.

Correspondence regarding the Gupta case

Nepalese newspaper Naya Patrika published details of WhatsApp correspondence between Phuyal and Sapkota concerning the case of Rohit Gupta, former director of Himalayan Reinsurance. Sapkota sent the justice a screenshot concerning a habeas corpus petition and asked him to stop it and dismiss the petition, claiming that the prime minister was allegedly interested in the matter.

Later, Phuyal told Sapkota that the panel of which he was a member had found insufficient grounds for Gupta's continued detention and ordered his release on bail of 20 million Nepalese rupees. After that, the justice suggested meeting the following day at Hotel Himalaya in Pulchowk.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Phuyal acknowledged that he had replied to Sapkota's messages and met with him. According to his version, Sapkota sent messages allegedly related to the prime minister's position, and after suspicions arose, he and other justices passed information about the contacts to the prime minister's secretariat. Phuyal also stated that the published materials reflect only part of the circumstances.

Information about possible transfers

Separately, materials about alleged money transfers mentioning Sharma, lawmaker Bishwaraj Pokharel and Banshiraj Dahal spread on social media. They refer to contributions totaling 198,333 in an unspecified currency over three months, as well as a request for an additional transfer of $7,500.

Sharma denied any involvement with Sapkota, the mentioned individuals or the described financial transactions. He stated that he does not know these people, had no direct or indirect contacts with them, and did not meet them. The Kathmandu Post notes that the materials circulating publicly may have been obtained by police from Sapkota's phone, but these claims are not established facts.

The Nepal Bar Association stressed that the reports must be verified on the basis of evidence, impartially and transparently. The organization stated that if violations are established, accountability must follow regardless of position, and if the allegations are not confirmed, the conclusions should protect people's reputations and the authority of judicial institutions.

title: Geopolitical Aspects Of Elections - The Rising Nepal
description: Geopolitical Aspects Of Elections  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Elections not only reframe internal power equations in national politics but also play a key role in recalibrating power hierarchies in international geopolitics. While they carry a strong national signature, their repercussions reverberate far beyond national borders. Election outcomes shape national politics and caution international powers to remain aware of their limitations. This article examines how the recent election results in Brazil, Serbia and Israel, alongside the upcoming elections in the USA, could potentially bring about a shift in the conflict-ridden realities of international geopolitics.

Former US House Speaker Tip O'Neill once remarked, "All politics is local", but the geopolitical ripples that the Brazilian and Serbian election results have set off prove that this is not always true. National politics is deeply connected with global power structures and a change in internal power equations automatically affects the entire architecture of international power politics.

Monroe Doctrine

The Brazilian election received unusual media spotlight, though elections in Latin American countries often attract more than a fair share of public attention than in other parts of the world because of deeply entrenched

American interest in the region. Historically, the United States views Latin America as its sphere of influence in line with the Monroe Doctrine, first articulated by former US President James Monroe on 2 December 1823. Throughout the 20th century, this doctrine served as a barrier against attempts at colonial expansion by European powers into the Western Hemisphere. Though the USA asserted less on the enforcement of this doctrine following the end of the colonial era, it continues to

leverage this principle even today to counter the economic and political expansion of influence of its emerging global and regional competitors.

In view of the geopolitical location, Brazil appears destined to live under the overbearing shadow of US influence despite Lula's claim in his victory speech that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard". Lula pulled off the stunning victory in the face of tremendous odds, especially with the US government openly opposing him and calling for the victory of his nemesis, Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, now in prison for attempting a coup against the elected government. The victory of Lula presents an unprecedented case also because he won the presidential election even after losing the polls in the first round. Geopolitical implications of Lula's victory are there, but the electoral turn of events have proved that ideology inevitably seeps through the iron curtain of force to influence the people's minds.

Brazil truly presented an electoral miracle, but it was not alone. On the other side of the Atlantic in Serbia, a grassroots organization called

Student List won the election by defeating populist leader Aleksandar Vucic by 141 seats as against 103 seats won by Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). Linking the elections with the decline of far-right politics noted historian and journalist Anne Applebaum commented on X, "In one day, two politicians –Bolsonaro in Brazil and Vucic in Serbia …have lost surprise election, thanks to high turnout. The rise of international far-right is not inevitable".

The electoral results in Brazil and Serbia, alongside the fluid landscape as revealed by the indecisive October 27 Israeli election, show that the neo-liberal global order is far from in ship shape. Whatever the outcomes of the ongoing shifts, they are expected to have far-reaching impact on the strategic global alignments and economic mobility. Amid escalating tensions between the belligerent parties, the specter of wider conflict looms large, as highlighted by Israel's repeated threats to launch another attack on Iran over the continued standoff on the latter's nuclear program. In response, Iran has also threatened to target airports, energy infrastructure, pipelines, undersea communication cables and American bases, increasing the risk of escalating conflict to a wider scale.

The Iran war jointly launched by Israel and the USA has already severely affected the energy supply through the Strait of Hormuz, leading to increased prices of fuel and other commodities. Inflation and high cost of living have already badly affected the lives of

people worldwide, including the

American people, turning day-to-day economic problems of the communities into major issues in internal electoral politics.

Popular intervention

The global community is tired of wars. All eyes are, therefore, riveted on the upcoming elections in these countries as an opportunity for a much-needed collective popular

intervention to compel their rulers to reverse course and pursue a peaceful way out through peaceful exercise of adult

franchise. Against overwhelming public

sentiment for peaceful settlement of conflict, the war in West Asia is threatening to assume apocalyptic proportions, with threats of using all kinds of weapons, including nuclear weapons, which could lead to unthinkable consequences for human civilization. The parties in

conflict must realize that war is no longer an issue exclusive to them. It is closely linked with the life of ordinary people who are losing access to food, energy, medicine, transport, and health care.

In all democratic countries, elections provide a vital opportunity for the

people to exercise their silent force to hold leaders accountable and ensure that the major issues of the day are resolved through dialogue and consent of the people. The results of elections in Brazil and Serbia demonstrate that voters can challenge the status quo to bring about a shift in the political course once considered irreversible.





(Dr. Bharadwaj is former ambassador and former chairperson of Gorkhapatra Corporation. bharadwajnarad@gmail.com)

title: Planners map a green transport blueprint for Nepal’s congested Kathmandu Valley - Bioengineer.org
description: Planners map a green transport blueprint for Nepal’s congested Kathmandu Valley  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Kathmandu Valley’s roads are choking on a flood of private vehicles, and a new planning-level study argues that a coordinated package of pedestrian zones, cycle lanes, electric buses and smart enforcement could begin to reverse the decline. The research, published as an open-access article in Discover Vehicles, focuses on the Gaushala-Ratopul corridor in Kathmandu Metropolitan City and lays out a phased framework for an integrated green urban transportation system tailored to the valley’s specific physical, institutional and cultural conditions. Its authors are careful to frame the work as a feasibility assessment rather than an engineering design: no traffic simulation, emission modelling or demand forecasting was performed, and the study explicitly identifies these as the highest-priority gaps for follow-up research.

The evidence base rests on structured field observation at four locations during weekday morning peak hours between 8:00 and 9:00 am, repeated over three sessions. Vehicle counts ranged from roughly 85 vehicles per hour on the narrow, heritage-adjacent Jaya Bageshwori Road to approximately 560 vehicles per hour on a segment of the Ring Road, the valley’s primary circumferential arterial. Motorcycles and microbuses dominated the traffic mix. At Gaushala Chowk, motorcycles made up about 52 percent of observed peak-hour flow, consistent with earlier work reporting that two-wheelers constitute over 70 percent of registered vehicles in Kathmandu Metropolitan City. At Ratopul Junction, microbuses accounted for roughly 38 percent, reflecting the node’s role on several informal public transport routes. Footpath conditions were graded on a descriptive scale, and the Ring Road segment fared worst, with vendor encroachment eliminating all usable pedestrian space along the observed stretch.

An origin-destination survey added a behavioural layer to the counts. Thirty-five respondents were recruited through purposive sampling across five stakeholder categories: fourteen daily commuters, eight shop owners, six students, four transport workers and three traffic police officers. Work-related commuting emerged as the dominant peak-hour trip purpose, with the Ratopul-Gaushala axis the most common origin-destination pair. Student trips between Gaushala and Pulchowk Campus, a distance of roughly four kilometres, formed the second-largest demand segment, a category the authors flag as having consistent potential for modal shift to cycling in comparable South Asian studies. The survey also revealed that much of the light traffic on Jaya Bageshwori Road consists of through vehicles using it as a shortcut to dodge congestion at the Gaushala Ring Road junction, a pattern that directly conflicts with the pilgrimage and pedestrian movement the heritage street serves.

Pedestrianisation of Jaya Bageshwori Road emerges as the most immediately actionable proposal. Four lines of evidence converge: a carriageway narrower than five metres between building lines in places, structurally unsuited to two-way mixed traffic; the confirmed shortcut through-traffic; a Walk Score of 94 out of 100 classifying the precinct as a ‘Walker’s Paradise’, though the authors caution that this index reflects destination density and connectivity rather than footpath quality or traffic safety, both found to be poor; and an existing Detailed Project Report process initiated by Kathmandu Metropolitan City for facade and public realm improvement in the area. The proposed measures include restricting feeder road access to residents, peripheral parking with a left-in-left-out pattern, three predefined bus stops, vehicle access permitted only between 20:00 and 08:00, and widening the Bhandarkhal Forest side road to carry displaced through traffic. An exploratory acceptance survey of eight accessible residents and business operators recorded positive opinions from six, or 75 percent of accessible respondents; two shop owners who declined to participate reacted negatively, and the authors stress the finding indicates a broadly receptive disposition rather than validated community consent.

Cycling infrastructure is proposed across three spatial typologies. Dedicated physically separated lanes would run along arterial roads, with 1.2-metre lanes on the existing 14-metre Ring Road cross-section and 1.6-metre lanes on a proposed expanded 26-metre cross-section, separated from vehicular lanes by a raised pedestrian walkway that doubles as a protective barrier and allows bus stop access without crossing the cycle lane. Greenway routes along river corridors, such as the Gongabu-Tribhuvan University riverside alignment, would offer full separation from motor traffic with minimal land acquisition. Heritage connectivity routes would link Basantapur to Swayambhunath through low-traffic historic streets. The authors note that Copenhagen and Amsterdam have sustained cycling mode shares of 25 to 62 percent, with research from those cities identifying physical separation from motor traffic as the single most important determinant of uptake. Complementary measures include bike boxes at signalised intersections at Maitighar, Labim Mall and Kalimati, raised crossings at Asan and Durbar Marg, and a bicycle-sharing network with docking stations at twelve locations. Feasibility, however, hinges on right-of-way availability, slope grades of 5 to 15 percent in some corridors, and monsoon flooding risk on river routes, all requiring engineering validation beyond this study.

On electrification, the study draws heavily on Shenzhen, China, which completed the full electrification of its 16,359-bus municipal fleet between 2009 and 2017 using national purchase subsidies, depot charging, night-time charging to shift demand to off-peak grid periods, and co-located passenger amenities. For Kathmandu, a three-site charging network is proposed at Mitrapark, near Sifal Ground and along the Ring Road, selected for proximity to high-density traffic generators and compatible land use, with formal grid capacity and transformer load analysis flagged as prerequisites. An EV Exchange Programme would offer trade-in discounts for diesel and petrol vehicles, zero-interest financing, free initial charging setup and extended warranties; EV sales in Nepal rose significantly after import duty reductions, which the authors cite as evidence of price elasticity. No-emission zones restricted to electric vehicles and non-motorised transport are proposed for heritage precincts including Durbar Squares and Swayambhu. Nepal’s advantage is underlined by the fact that over 90 percent of its electricity comes from hydropower, giving EV charging a substantially lower lifecycle carbon footprint than in fossil-fuel-dependent grids.

Public transport proposals centre on two bus rapid transit corridors selected for carriageway width, left-lane availability and manageable intersection density: an eastern loop running Maitighar-Bhadrakali-RNAC-Jamal-KamalPokhari-Gaushala-Airport-Tinkune, and an urban core loop along the Thamel-Lainchaur-Bishnumati corridor-Teku-Tripureshwor axis. The study treats Nepal’s first BRT corridor, launched in September 2023 between Suryabinayak and Ratna Park with a dedicated lane for 25 buses during peak hours, as a cautionary precedent: when the lane conversion cut carriageway for remaining traffic, severe congestion drew public criticism and demands for reversal. The authors attribute the failure to missing preconditions, including mixed-traffic interaction modelling, last-mile connectivity planning, demand estimation and phased implementation, lessons echoed by Delhi’s BRT corridor experience from 2008 to 2016. Formal ridership projections and intersection delay modelling are identified as essential before either new corridor can be approved.

The smart-management and integration layer proposes Automatic Number Plate Recognition combined with CCTV at key intersections to automate detection of speeding, red-light running and illegal parking, generating penalty notices dispatched with online payment links and escalating penalties for non-compliance, mirroring systems deployed in Singapore and Indian metropolitan areas. Three institutional prerequisites are named: a digitised vehicle registration database linked to the Department of Transport Management, reliable network connectivity, and a legal framework for electronic fines and digital evidence. A pilot at Gaushala Chowk, Ratopul Junction and the Ring Road junction is suggested before valley-wide rollout. Shared cycle and moped docking at transit nodes, educational institutions and commercial hubs would tackle first-last-mile gaps, since many trips originate or end more than 500 metres from the nearest stop, and a unified digital mobility platform would layer real-time bus tracking, seat availability, digital fares and multi-modal route planning, building on the existing Sajha Plus application.

The framework is organised into short-term actions of zero to two years, designed to be low-cost, reversible and aligned with existing municipal processes, including an electric bus pilot on the Ratna Park-Thamel route; medium-term actions of two to five years requiring inter-agency coordination and likely international climate finance or public-private partnerships; and long-term actions of five to ten years contingent on demonstrated success and legislative backing. Revenue streams and funding mechanisms, from government budgets and Green Climate Fund or Global Environment Facility instruments to congestion pricing modelled on London and Stockholm, corporate sponsorship and green bonds, are laid out conceptually, with a formal financial viability assessment recommended as a prerequisite for later phases. Alignment with Sustainable Development Goals 6, 7 and 11 is mapped through indicator linkages grounded in international precedent rather than local quantification.

The authors are unusually explicit about the study’s boundaries. Vehicle counts are observational estimates from limited weekday morning sessions and must not be used for engineering design without standardised counts over at least seven days including weekends and seasonal variation. No emission modelling or air quality assessment was performed, no ridership projections were produced, and the survey samples of 35 and 8 respondents are too small for statistical inference; a follow-up pedestrianisation study with at least 400 respondents is recommended. Cost estimates, benefit-cost analysis, right-of-way verification and stakeholder representation gaps, including the absence of transport union and provincial government voices, are all acknowledged. Within those limits, the study offers Kathmandu Valley a structured analytical foundation: a corridor-specific baseline, a portfolio of interventions each anchored to demonstrated precedents in comparable cities, and a clear agenda of quantitative research needed to move from planning-level feasibility to engineering design and investment decisions.

title: Nepal plans temporary bridges to reopen flood-hit Rasuwagadhi border crossing - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal plans temporary bridges to reopen flood-hit Rasuwagadhi border crossing  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Rasuwagadhi border crossing with China has been cut off since floods on August 26, with no clear timeline for reopening. More than two months on, the road to the crossing remains incomplete, with bridges washed away and essential infrastructure yet to be restored.

So when will the crossing reopen? Neither the Department of Customs nor the Department of Roads has a definite answer.

Work is underway to prepare the foundations for a Bailey bridge over the Bhotekoshi river at Syaphrubesi. Vijay Jaisi, director general of the Department of Roads, said the bridge was expected to be installed before Tihar, the Hindu festival that falls in early November.

“After that, we need to install four Bailey bridges between Syaphrubesi and the Rasuwagadhi border,” he said. “The immediate priority is to open a temporary road track to the border and make it easier for people and vehicles to move.”

A permanent road will be planned after further studies, Jaisi said. The immediate goal is to reconnect communities cut off by the floods, followed by a feasibility study for a lasting road link. The department has sought the finance ministry’s approval to proceed with the study, he added.

The closure has disrupted a key trade route between Nepal and China. Rasuwagadhi has been a major entry point for electric vehicles, which account for 60 percent of imports through the crossing, according to customs data. Other goods imported through the route include electrical equipment, ready-made garments, footwear, agricultural products, telecommunications equipment, machinery for hydropower projects, vehicles and industrial machinery.

Located about 152 kilometres north of Kathmandu, Rasuwagadhi has long played a central role in Nepal-China trade, revenue collection, border management and economic ties.

The customs office was established there in 1956 to facilitate trade between communities in Rasuwa and the Kerung area of Tibet, including the exchange of goods for everyday needs and the collection of customs revenue, according to the office’s website.

The crossing gained prominence after the April 2015 earthquake severely disrupted the Tatopani route in Sindhupalchok, then a major gateway for Nepal-China trade. Rasuwagadhi subsequently emerged as the country’s principal northern trade route. Its importance grew further after China recognised it as an international border crossing in 2017, according to the Rasuwa Customs Office.

But the route has suffered repeated damage. On July 8, 2025, flooding in the Lhende river along the Nepal-China border swept away the Miteri Bridge. The floods also destroyed the customs yard at Timure, carrying away vehicles and containers and causing substantial losses.

The crossing reopened on January 1, 2026, after remaining closed for nearly six months. It is now once again out of operation, with the latest destruction raising questions about how the route should be rebuilt. “We will study how to build a permanent road and consult experts before moving ahead with construction,” Jaisi said. “We also asked the Chinese government to open a track towards Syaphrubesi from the Rasuwagadhi side as an immediate measure, but no work has been done, and we have received no further information.”

Construction of a bridge at Syaphrubesi is a prerequisite for opening the road track towards the border, said Krishna Nath Ojha, project chief of the Galchhi-Trishuli-Mailung-Syaphrubesi -Rasuwagadhi Road Project, based in Bidur. Work on the track and the installation of Bailey bridges will proceed as required, he said.

Sushil Babu Dhakal, chief of the Development Assistance Coordination and Quality Division under the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure Development, said officials from Nepal and China had an understanding that the old crossing should be restored.

However, key decisions about the facilities needed to resume operations remain pending. “No decision has been made on where to relocate the customs and immigration offices, and China has not yet communicated its position on the matter,” Dhakal said. “We will have to decide whether to rebuild them at the old site or establish them somewhere else.”

An eight-member Chinese technical team is also assessing the flood damage around Rasuwagadhi, he said.

An expressway instead of a railway?

The government is also considering a longer-term alternative to repeatedly rebuilding roads damaged by major floods: an expressway linking Kathmandu and Kerung, potentially replacing the proposed cross-border railway.

“The Kathmandu-Kerung railway corridor had been studied as a long-term solution, but there is now also a proposal to study an expressway instead of a railway,” Dhakal said.

The proposed road could include tunnels, bridges and elevated sections, depending on the terrain and engineering requirements. The aim would be to build infrastructure capable of withstanding or bypassing extreme flooding similar to the recent disaster, he said. “How high the road would need to be built, how much it would cost and how long construction would take will become clear only after a detailed study,” Dhakal said.

Before the floods, work was underway with Chinese grant assistance to upgrade the 16-kilometre road between Syaphrubesi and Rasuwagadhi into a two-lane highway. The damage has made it impossible to simply resume construction along the original alignment, he said.

A Chinese technical team that includes structural engineers and geotechnical experts will examine the site to assess possible routes, construction challenges and the feasibility of rebuilding the road, Dhakal said. The team came after Nepal requested technical advice from China on restoring the Rasuwagadhi corridor. It had visited the Korala border crossing in Mustang before Dashain and was preparing to inspect Rasuwagadhi.

“China is positive about rebuilding the road and reopening the crossing,” Dhakal said. “Its importance is also clear because it is an international border crossing.”

title: Middlemen reap Tanahun flower profits - The Rising Nepal
description: Middlemen reap Tanahun flower profits  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Amarraj Naharki, Tanahun, Oct. 30: Commercial flower farmers in Tanahun are facing mounting concerns over unsold produce and rain damage as Tihar approaches. Although demand for marigolds rises during the festive season, farmers are uncertain whether they will receive fair prices for their produce.

Farmers say changing weather patterns, including rainfall during the winter months, have increased the risk of flowers being damaged just as they are ready for harvesting. The gap between the prices received by producers and those paid by consumers has widened, with farmers selling flowers at low prices while consumers pay considerably more in the market. Limited direct access to markets has allowed intermediaries to capture a substantial share of the profits. The experience of a group of women growing marigolds collectively in Chhimliswara of Myagde Rural Municipality-4, Tanahun, illustrates the problem.

The 23 women affiliated with the Chandeshwari Fruit and Vegetable Producers' Group have been cultivating flowers on 16 ropanis of land. However, they have struggled to secure fair prices for their produce. Group chairperson Jitmaya Rana said farmers sold marigolds for Rs. 300 per kilogram, while the same flowers fetched between Rs. 800 and Rs. 1,000 per kilogram in the market. "We work hard to grow the flowers, but we do not receive a fair price when it comes to selling them. We have to sell them for Rs. 300 per kilogram, while middlemen sell the same flowers for between Rs. 800 and Rs. 1,000,"

Rana said.

Despite the seasonal increase in demand, the lack of guaranteed markets has raised concerns that farmers may struggle even to recover their investment.

Farmers said rainfall during the harvesting period could damage flower quality, while storing harvested flowers safely was also difficult. These risks could further affect sales and earnings.

Rana said farmers had traditionally expected little rainfall during winter, but changing weather patterns had made both production and income increasingly unpredictable. Myagde Rural Municipality chairperson Shri Prasad Shrestha said the local government had been supporting farmers and groups involved in flower farming in Wards 4, 5 and 6.

He said the rural municipality had adopted a policy of increasing the use of locally grown flowers during its own programmes and festivals to help expand the market for local produce.

According to Shrestha, group-based flower farming is practised in Chhimliswara in Ward No. 4 and Dharapani in Ward No. 5, while Santosh Shrestha has been cultivating flowers commercially in Ward No. 6.

The women began commercial flower farming last year with support from the rural municipality and guidance from agricultural technicians.

title: Conquering War And Cancer - The Rising Nepal
description: Conquering War And Cancer  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Yuddha Ladey, Cancer Jitey, is a memoir by Lila Sharma, 'Asmita', a Maoist combatant who rose to the position of brigade vice-commander during Nepal’s civil war. Born and raised in Dang, Sharma joined the Maoist movement as a woman. She kept diaries during the war. Later, she used her memories to write this book. Published by Publication Nepalaya in 2026, the memoir explores her experiences during the conflict, struggles after the war and battle with cancer. Rather than presenting only the heroic or tragic sides of war, she portrays a life shaped by political ideals, personal struggles and unexpected challenges.

The beginning of the book is touching because of Sharma’s dream of studying ANM (Auxiliary Nurse Midwifery). However, on the day of submitting her application form, a flood in the Rapti River disrupted her plans, forcing her to return home in tears. This incident may connect with readers because everyone has a story or an unfulfilled wish. Before becoming a combatant, Sharma was simply a girl with dreams for her future. Her story reminds readers that behind every identity lies a past filled with hopes, disappointments and possibilities that never came true.

One of the important aspects of this memoir is its portrayal of women in war. The experiences of combatants are often discussed less than political events and military strategies. Sharma highlights the challenges women faced on the battlefield during menstruation and pregnancy. Women had to continue fighting during their periods, endure circumstances during pregnancy and manage the responsibilities of motherhood. Despite these challenges, they were often considered weaker than men. Through her experiences, Sharma questions this assumption and demonstrates that women can be equally courageous and capable in difficult situations. This perspective is valuable because such personal realities are often missing from accounts of Nepal’s war.

However, some moments may be difficult for readers to accept fully. In one battlefield scene, bullets rain down from helicopters and fighters are dying, yet Sharma describes her fellow fighter, Sonu, smiling while sharing the last drops of her water. Although this moment may represent humanity and solidarity, the portrayal seems dramatic. In such a situation, fear, panic and the instinct to survive are natural responses. Presenting the scene through a heroic moment risks making war seem cinematic. Although courage and kindness can exist amid violence, the psychological trauma and terror could have been explored more deeply.

Another question concerns Sharma’s repeated statements that she did not want to join the war and would have refused to move between shelters at night if the instruction had come from her parents rather than her leaders. She became a brigade vice-commander and performed her duties on the battlefield. How did someone initially unwilling to participate in war become a combatant? Perhaps she adapted to her circumstances, developed a sense of duty or became committed to a role she had never intended to take. These experiences are not necessarily contradictory. A deeper explanation of this transformation would have made her psychological journey more convincing.

Beyond the battlefield, the memoir raises questions about former combatants’ lives after the war. Many returned to society without education, professional skills or stable employment. Having sacrificed their youth for ideals of equality and justice, they had to question whether their struggles had fulfilled those promises. The psychological consequences of war do not disappear with a peace agreement. Former combatants must confront their memories, find work, support their families and rebuild their identities. Sharma’s reflections reveal the gap between promises and the everyday realities of those who fought for them.

This also encourages reflection on Nepal’s history. Regardless of changing parties, governments or revolutions, ordinary citizens often bear the greatest burden. From a Marxist perspective, the continuing exploitation of the proletariat by the bourgeoisie helps explain this contradiction. People with resources and less power often suffer the most, while those holding political and economic power can better protect their interests. After major political transformations, inequalities based on class, caste and gender persist in Nepali society. The question is not simply whether a revolution succeeded politically but whether it fulfilled its promises to those who sacrificed their lives and futures for it.

Sharma’s observations on feminism expose the gap between what people say and practise. Although combatants advocated gender equality, Sharma describes how she and her team left the dishes they had used after a programme for Vauju, the wife of Badri Dai, to clean. This incident is both satirical and realistic. It shows how people can speak about equality publicly while continuing practices privately. Feminism cannot be limited to speeches, slogans or political programmes; it must also be reflected in behaviour. This small incident conveys a message about the hypocrisy that can exist even among those who claim to fight for equality.

Although the title suggests that cancer will be a focus, this part of the memoir receives less attention than readers might expect. Most of the narrative focuses on the war and Sharma’s experiences as a combatant. Readers may expect a detailed account of cancer treatment, emotional struggles and coping mechanisms. Those seeking guidance or deeper insight into surviving cancer may feel disappointed. A fuller exploration of her fears, treatment difficulties, family’s emotional burden and sources of strength could have offered encouragement to cancer patients and their families. A balanced account of both struggles would have strengthened the memoir.

Overall, Yuddha Ladey, Cancer Jitey is a meaningful memoir that explores women’s experiences during Nepal’s civil war, post-war struggles, gender inequality, class differences and the psychological effects of conflict. Its strength lies in using experiences to reveal the gap between revolutionary promises and reality. However, some battlefield scenes could have explored emotions more deeply. Sharma’s initial reluctance to join the war needed clearer explanation, and her cancer journey deserved greater attention. Still, the memoir offers lessons about war, lost dreams and rebuilding life.

(A novice poet, Shakya writes on various issues.)

title: Who Pays For Nepal’s Transition? - The Rising Nepal
description: Who Pays For Nepal’s Transition?  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Picture a welder from the Terai who has spent most of his working life on Gulf oil and gas sites. His earnings built the family house and kept his children in school. Now his company is cutting jobs, and he is coming home with a bad back, no pension and no plan.

Meanwhile, in Nepal, a mechanic who has repaired petrol engines for decades watches more electric cars pass his workshop, while fewer customers walk in. The welder and the mechanic did little to cause climate change. Yet they may be among the first to lose their jobs as the world moves away from oil and petrol.

This is what "just transition" is about: moving to clean energy in a way that is fair to workers and communities. Nepal wants roads, factories and jobs, but it has also promised the world a cleaner path.

The idea is not new. Trade unions first raised it, and the 2015 Paris Agreement, signed at the COP21 climate summit, included it. At COP30 in Belém, Brazil, last November, countries agreed to set up a Just Transition Mechanism, but attached to it was no new money. None of this forces a least developed country like Nepal to act.

Yet Nepal has gone further than many. At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, Nepal promised to reach net-zero emissions by 2045, which means removing as much carbon as it releases. Nepal's latest UN climate plan, NDC 3.0, also promises to study which workers will be affected and to make a plan to protect them. The Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment will lead this work.

The problem is money. Nepal's own plan says it needs USD 73.74 billion, and 85 per cent of it must come from other countries. If that money comes as loans, Nepal will have to pay it back, though it did little to cause climate change. The real test is whether the welder and the mechanic are actually protected.

Rich countries became rich by burning coal and oil and cleaned up later. Some economists say poor countries should be allowed to do the same. But Nepal is different. Almost all its electricity already comes from its rivers, so growing clean can also mean growing cheaper.

In the first ten months of FY 2024/25, Nepal imported petroleum worth Rs. 223 billion and earned Rs. 92.51 billion in revenue from it, according to the Department of Customs. So every litre of fuel Nepal stops importing saves foreign currency but also means less tax money for the government.

Nepal's economy is also unusual. Most countries move from farming to factories and then to services. The country largely skipped the factory stage, jumping from farming to services and money sent home by workers abroad.

Workers at home

Many Nepalis work in jobs that release a lot of greenhouse gases: cement factories, brick kilns, transport, and the mechanics and fuel attendants who keep petrol vehicles running. Much of this work is informal, without securities, with no contract, no pension and no insurance.

Though some factories now control dust and spray water to keep the air cleaner, the issue is prominent in many factories. The International Labour Organisation has already warned that extreme heat caused by climate change is now a health danger at work, especially outdoors.

For mechanics, change has already arrived. According to the government's National Transport Policy, over 70 per cent of private cars imported into Nepal are now electric, ranking Nepal second only to Norway. But motorcycles, mostly petrol, make up over 80 per cent of all vehicles on the road, so the benefits so far go mainly to better-off city families.

Hydropower is renewable, but it is not always sustainable. Larger projects have pushed local villages and indigenous communities off their land, questioning their rights and leaving them behind. Climate change-induced rapid melting glaciers have threatened the dams and are also leading to scarcity in the winter, affecting the water ecosystem.

Foreign employment

Nepal's story does not end at its borders. Money sent home by migrant workers equalled 27.8 per cent of GDP in FY 2024/25, according to the Ministry of Finance's Economic Survey. Much of it comes from Gulf and Asian economies built on oil and gas.

The Gulf states will not stop pumping oil overnight. As those economies change, workers may return without any benefit, and many may carry the hidden burden of poor mental health.

The government should have a proper plan to settle returnees from foreign countries. Whether workers come back from the Gulf or become unemployed at home, they need a safety net. The provision of health insurance, pension and unemployment benefits would prevent a breakdown of a family's finances, but casual workers and returning migrants rarely possess these safeguards.

There is no just transition without people's rights and representation. Workers, indigenous communities, women and returning migrants must have a say in decisions. And new jobs must be ready before old ones disappear. Closing one door before opening another is not a transition. It is abandonment.

First, identify the stakeholders who will be affected before deciding when to discontinue petrol and diesel use. Second, promote the creation of cleaner energy businesses within the country. Nepal may not be able to compete with China in solar panel and battery production, and restricting cheap imports will only slow down the transition to electric cars.

However, the country can assemble electric vehicles, repair and recycle batteries, and set up charging stations, which a retrained mechanic can manage. Others can venture into small-scale clean energy enterprises, such as solar panel repair or food processing, or into modern agriculture, if they are given appropriate training and access to credit.

Third, promoting the conversion of factory and household machinery to use locally produced electricity instead of imported fuels will reduce the country’s carbon footprint. For example, cement and brick manufacturing companies can adopt electric machines and utilise solar panels. Housewives can also do away with gas cylinders and firewood and cook with electric stoves, thus cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions.

This initiative will have a significant impact on Nepalese society because it will free women from the drudgery of collecting firewood and subjecting their families to smoke inhalation. In the government, it is important that we promote things like electric buses, scooters, and stoves before we go down to the level of individual car ownership.

Fourth, we must not depend on huge hydro projects. Roof-mounted solar panels, miniature hydro projects, and village-level electricity generation will augment the use of modern equipment in factories, lighting in houses, and brick-making in kilns, while cutting down on waste.

Laying more power lines should be prioritised, and electricity exports should be regarded as a bonus. Finally, requesting development grants from developed countries, instead of loans, will ease the burden of repayment.

Ultimately, a just transition entails good work and good life principles that give meaning to people’s lives. The process of transitioning to a net-zero energy economy in Nepal will be challenging and full of hard choices. But if it keeps people at the centre, it can show that a small developing country can move to clean energy fairly.

Clean energy without justice is simply a new way of leaving people behind. The welder and the mechanic deserve better, and Nepal has the chance to prove it.

title: Japan cites privacy in withholding details on Nepal’s envoy nominee - The Kathmandu Post
description: Japan cites privacy in withholding details on Nepal’s envoy nominee  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The parliamentary hearing committee is preparing to convene a meeting to decide on the nomination of Jigyan Kumar Thapa as Nepal’s ambassador to Japan. Under the law, the committee must complete the hearing process within 45 days of receiving a nomination. It has until November 5 to decide on Thapa. If it fails to send its decision within that period, there will be no legal obstacle to his appointment.

Committee secretary Tul Bahadur Kandel said a meeting had been proposed for Monday to discuss and decide on Thapa’s nomination.

Questions were raised during the hearing about whether Thapa holds permanent residency in Japan. The committee subsequently wrote twice to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, seeking details from the Japanese government. The ministry then instructed Nepal’s embassy in Tokyo to establish whether Thapa had renounced his Japanese permanent residency and whether he had received payments or benefits from Japanese government funds.

Japanese authorities, however, said they could not provide the information because it concerned an individual’s privacy, according to foreign ministry officials. “We learnt, while following up with ministry officials, that Japan had responded that it could not disclose personal information,” committee chair Bodh Narayan Shrestha told Kantipur. “We have asked the ministry to send us a written response on the matter.”

The committee first wrote to the foreign ministry on October 11, seeking details about Thapa’s financial obligations and permanent residency status. After the ministry’s request to Nepal’s embassy in Japan went unanswered, the committee sent a second letter to the ministry on October 26, asking it to follow up with the embassy. The ministry also sent a second letter to the embassy that day, seeking information about Thapa’s involvement with Japanese government agencies.

In the personal details he submitted to the parliamentary hearing committee and the foreign ministry, Thapa listed his work with organisations including the Kanagawa International Foundation (KIF) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency. He also acknowledged working with Japanese government ministries, universities and other organisations.

“Since it has been decided to conduct further investigations into whether he received any appointment from Japanese government agencies in connection with these responsibilities, and whether he received remuneration or other benefits from public funds, the committee requests that documents clarifying these matters be sought from the relevant official agencies of the Japanese government and made available to the committee,” the hearing committee said in its letter to the foreign ministry.

The ministry forwarded the request to Nepal’s embassy in Japan, instructing it to obtain the documents from the relevant Japanese government agencies and send them to Kathmandu as soon as possible.

A foreign ministry official confirmed that the committee had been informed that Japan would not provide details about Thapa’s financial dealings, family and personal circumstances. The official said the controversy had arisen partly because Thapa had been nominated as ambassador to the very country whose permanent residency status and official records were under scrutiny.

The official added that the lack of a response despite two rounds of correspondence with Japan had put Nepal in a diplomatically difficult position.

“We had doubts about whether the Japanese government would share an individual’s personal details with another country,” the official said. “There was also the question of whether the Nepal government itself would readily share the personal information of a foreign national with another country.”

The Cabinet proposed ambassadors for 13 countries on September 18. The Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers registered their names with the parliamentary hearing committee on September 23.

Under Rule 26(2) of the Federal Parliament Joint Meeting and Committee (Operation) Rules, 2024, the committee must conduct hearings on the proposed nominees and send its decision to the relevant authority within 45 days of receiving the names. The rule states that if the committee fails to communicate its decision within that period, there will be no obstacle to the appointment of the nominees to the proposed positions.

If the committee does not decide on Thapa’s nomination by November 5, the appointment process could therefore proceed under the rules.

Committee chair Shrestha said the nomination had also raised questions about a potential conflict of interest. The directive governing ambassadorial appointments states that candidates must not hold permanent or temporary residency permits, or enjoy residency-related facilities, in a foreign country. It also requires that they have no conflicting interests in the country to which they are appointed.

Shrestha said the delay stemmed from the government’s failure to carry out adequate background checks before recommending candidates.

“The government appears not to have properly examined the background of the person it nominated,” he said.

Shrestha said the committee would not clear the way for Thapa’s automatic appointment simply by allowing the deadline to pass.

“The parliamentary hearing committee is sovereign in itself, and there is agreement among all members that it must exercise its authority,” he said. “We will make a decision, either to reject or endorse the nomination, within 45 days.”

The committee had suspended its meeting on October 14 after Thapa’s nomination was put to a vote. The meeting was adjourned after lawmakers from the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party argued that his nomination should be rejected and that the meeting should be suspended.

That day, the committee rejected two of the 13 nominees, Giri Bahadur Sunar, proposed as ambassador to Saudi Arabia, and Chudamani Kharel, proposed for Malaysia. The other 10 nominees were endorsed.

A senior foreign ministry source claimed that Speaker DP Aryal had recommended Thapa’s name for the ambassadorship. According to the source, concerns had been raised at the time that appointing Thapa to Japan could trigger questions about a conflict of interest and his permanent residency status. The source said the government had nevertheless proceeded with the nomination under pressure from the Speaker.

A member of the hearing committee said Aryal had also held several discussions with committee chair Shrestha and Kabindra Burlakoti, the RSP’s chief whip and a committee member, as the panel prepared to decide on Thapa’s nomination.

The member said Thapa had been asked to withdraw his name after the controversy emerged but had refused to do so.

Speaking to Kantipur, Thapa confirmed that the committee had asked him to consider withdrawing his nomination.

During his hearing, Thapa said he had renounced his Japanese permanent residency in March to become Nepal’s ambassador to Japan. His wife and sons, however, continue to hold Japanese permanent residency.

The foreign ministry has informally conveyed to the committee the response received through Nepal’s embassy in Japan. The committee is preparing to call a meeting and take a decision after receiving the ministry’s formal written response.

Committee secretary Kandel said the meeting had been proposed to discuss and decide on Thapa’s nomination.

“The ministry has informed us that Japan responded that the details requested by the committee concern personal privacy and cannot be shared,” he said. “We have asked the ministry to send us that response in writing.”

In its letter to Nepal’s embassy in Japan, the foreign ministry also sought proof that Thapa had renounced his Japanese permanent residency.

The United Nations General Assembly has unanimously approved a three-year extension to the preparatory period for Nepal and Bangladesh to graduate from the category of Least Developed Countries (LDCs), giving both countries until November 24, 2029, to prepare for the transition.

The General Assembly decided at its 81st session in New York, following a proposal jointly pursued by the two countries. The assembly unanimously adopted Resolution 81/L.8, extending their preparatory periods.

Khalilur Rahman, president of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly and Bangladesh’s foreign minister, said the extension recognised the economic uncertainties, external shocks and persistent vulnerabilities facing the two countries. “This extension is not a retreat, but an investment in lasting progress. Graduation should advance development, not disrupt it,” he said. “Success must be measured not by time gained, but by resilience built, reforms delivered and development secured.”

Nepal formally sought the extension in May this year, arguing that it needed more time to strengthen its economic resilience, productive capacity and institutional preparedness before losing the special support measures available to LDCs.

Nepal had been scheduled to graduate from the category on November 24, 2026, following a General Assembly decision in November 2021. The assembly had granted the country an exceptional five-year preparatory period, rather than the usual three years, in recognition of the economic and social disruptions caused by the Covid-19 pandemic.

The latest decision pushes Nepal’s graduation date back by another three years.

Nepal’s efforts to graduate from the LDC category, a status it has held since 1971, have faced repeated delays. The country first met the UN’s graduation criteria in 2015, but the government sought a deferral in 2018, citing the economic and social setbacks caused by the devastating 2015 earthquake and subsequent disasters. The UN Committee for Development Policy agreed to defer the recommendation.

In its 2021 triennial review, the committee again recommended Nepal’s graduation after the country met the required thresholds for the Human Assets Index (HAI) and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI). Although Nepal’s gross national income per capita remained below the required threshold, it qualified under the UN’s graduation rules by meeting the other two criteria.

The General Assembly endorsed the recommendation on November 24, 2021, giving Nepal five years to prepare for graduation because of the pandemic's economic disruptions.

As the 2026 deadline approached, however, the government concluded that Nepal was not adequately prepared to cope with the economic consequences of losing international support measures reserved for LDCs.

On May 13, 2026, Nepal formally requested the chair of the Committee for Development Policy to extend its preparatory period until November 2029. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs cited changing domestic and international economic and political circumstances, geopolitical tensions, disruptions to global supply chains and their potential impact on remittance inflows as reasons for the request.

The government also raised concerns about the possible loss of duty-free and quota-free market access for Nepali exports, delays in implementing the Smooth Transition Strategy and the country’s limited productive and institutional capacity. Studies cited by the government projected that employment in productive sectors could decline by as much as 35 percent after graduation without adequate transition measures.

Adopted in February 2024, Nepal’s Smooth Transition Strategy identifies six priority areas: macroeconomic stability; trade and investment; economic transformation; productive capacity; climate change and disaster risk management; and social inclusion. It aims to minimise the adverse effects of graduation while helping the country benefit from new development opportunities.

The additional three years are expected to give Nepal more time to implement the strategy, strengthen its economic foundations, improve competitiveness and prepare for the eventual withdrawal of international support measures available exclusively to LDCs.

Nepal has said it will use the extended period to strengthen productive capacity and institutions, accelerate economic and social transformation, and ensure effective implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Doha Programme of Action.

title: Nagdhunga tunnel road to levy toll charges from Nov. 1 - The Rising Nepal
description: Nagdhunga tunnel road to levy toll charges from Nov. 1  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Oct. 30: Motorists using the Nagdhunga Tunnel road will have to pay toll charges from November 1, 2026.

The Nagdhunga Tunnel Construction Project, under the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, announced the introduction of the road user fee through a public notice.

The toll collection will begin in accordance with a decision taken by the executive committee of the Road Board Nepal on September 28 and a notice published in the Nepal Gazette, according to Deputy Project Director and information officer Sanjaya Panthi of the Project.

The project has classified vehicles into four categories, with different toll rates for vehicles entering Kathmandu and those leaving the capital.

For Category 1 vehicles, including cars, vans, pick-ups, tractors, microbuses and other light vehicles, the toll charge will be Rs. 65 for entering Kathmandu and Rs. 60 for leaving the capital.

For Category 2 vehicles, comprising minibuses and mini-tippers or trucks, the charge will be Rs. 115 for entering Kathmandu and Rs. 80 for leaving

the capital. For Category 3 vehicles, including buses and trucks with a single rear axle, the toll will be Rs. 260 for entering Kathmandu and Rs. 200 for leaving the capital.

For Category 4 vehicles, including multi-axle trucks, other multi-axle vehicles and heavy equipment, the charge will be Rs. 600 for entering Kathmandu and Rs. 250 for leaving the capital.

Multi-axle vehicles entering Kathmandu will face the highest toll charge of Rs. 600, while cars and other light vehicles will pay the lowest rate of Rs. 60 to leave the capital.

publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
A spell of exceptionally clear weather brought bright blue skies, stunning mountain views, and pollution-less air to Nepal over Dasain and into this week, raising the spirits of a nation healing from back-to-back flood disasters from August-October.

But the clement weather did not last. Cyclone Arnab from the Bay of Bengal is forecast to dump heavy rain and snow on Friday-Saturday. After that, with the change in wind direction, smoke and smog from the south will start blowing into Nepal.

This drone photo shows the brightly-lit Kirtipur Stadium preparing for a Nepal Premier League (NPL) match on Tuesday evening as the sun set over the Central Himalayan peaks. The tournament is now recognised by the International Cricket Council (ICC) under the T20 setup.

Pakistan Cricket Board’s last-minute notice requiring a $25,000 fee per player to issue No Objection Certificates (NOCs) disallowed Pakistani cricketers from playing in Nepal, hurting what could have been a display of South Asian solidarity and celebration of the sport.

Nepali cricketers have performed well in matches abroad lately, and the national teams have carried the hopes of a nation bruised by disasters. The RSP government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah similarly carries the collective aspirations of Nepalis.

On Monday, when PM Shah inaugurated the tournament, smiling and waving to cheering spectators, some were quick to draw comparisons between his match attendance to disdain of Parliament and disregard for members of his own party as well as the opposition.

Photo: PMO NEPAL

The spirit of cricket is defined by teamwork, fair play, and sportsmanship. It offers an important lesson for politics that transcends populism and popularity, to performance on the pitch. It is a lesson Nepal’s past leaders ignored to their own peril.

PM Shah wants to be different. His party already has a two-thirds majority, it does not need to govern with threats, arrogance and social media stunts. Facebook likes and shares will only go so far.

The tournament offers a symbolic takeaway about teamwork. Nepalis hope Balen Shah plays a captain’s innings.
